Introduction to ReactJS

React (also known as React.js or ReactJS) is an open-source JavaScript library for building user interfaces (UIs), particularly single-page applications. Developed and maintained by Facebook, it emphasizes a component-based architecture, allowing developers to create reusable and modular UI elements.

Key aspects of React include:

  • Component-Based Architecture: UIs are built from isolated, reusable pieces of code called components. These components can manage their own state and render specific parts of the UI.
  • Declarative Programming: React focuses on a declarative approach, meaning you describe what you want the UI to look like based on the current state, and React handles the updates to efficiently render it.
  • Virtual DOM: React utilizes a virtual DOM, which is a lightweight copy of the actual browser DOM. When data changes, React updates the virtual DOM first, then efficiently calculates the minimal changes needed to update the real DOM, leading to improved performance.
  • JSX: React often uses JSX (JavaScript XML), a syntax extension that allows writing HTML-like code within JavaScript, making it more intuitive to define UI structures within components. While optional, it is widely adopted.
  • Unidirectional Data Flow: Data typically flows in a single direction in React applications, making it easier to understand and debug how data changes affect the UI.

ReactJS Environment Setup

Before running a React application, you must configure a ReactJS development environment. This guide provides step-by-step instructions for installing and setting up a fully functional React development setup.

Prior Requirement

Ensure that Node.js is installed on your system. React depends on Node.js and npm (Node Package Manager) to run and manage packages. Once installed, we can create a React project using a boilerplate.

  • Windows: Download the installer from Node.js official website and follow the setup wizard.
  • Mac: Use the Node.js installer from the official website or Homebrew brew install node.
  • Linux: Use your distribution’s package manager, e.g., sudo apt install nodejs npm for Ubuntu/Debian.

Create a React App using Vite

  1. Navigate to the folder where you want to create the project and open the terminal.
  2. Create the project: Run the following command: 
    npm create vite@latest <your-project-name>
  3. Select framework: Choose React and the variant JavaScript.
  4. Navigate to project folder: 
    cd <your-project-name>
  5. Run the React app: Start the development server using: 
    npm run dev

Once the server is running, you can open your browser and visit http://localhost:5173 to see your React app.

React JS ReactDOM

ReactDOM is a core package within the React ecosystem, specifically designed to interact with the Document Object Model (DOM) in web browsers. While React itself is a library for building user interfaces, ReactDOM provides the necessary methods to render those React components into the actual browser DOM and manage their updates.

Key aspects of React DOM include:

  • Rendering Components: It provides methods like createRoot() (for modern React versions) or render() (for older versions) to mount React components into a specified DOM element, making them visible in the browser.
  • DOM-specific APIs: ReactDOM offers APIs for tasks specific to web environments, such as managing focus, scroll position, or preloading resources, which are not part of core React.
  • Virtual DOM Reconciliation: ReactDOM plays a crucial role in the reconciliation process. It efficiently updates the real DOM by comparing the virtual DOM tree (React's in-memory representation) with the actual DOM and applying only the necessary changes.
  • JSX: React often uses JSX (JavaScript XML), a syntax extension that allows writing HTML-like code within JavaScript, making it more intuitive to define UI structures within components. While optional, it is widely adopted.
  • Unidirectional Data Flow: Data typically flows in a single direction in React applications, making it easier to understand and debug how data changes affect the UI.

Import React DOM using following command

import ReactDOM from 'react-dom';

React JSX

JSX stands for JavaScript XML. JSX is a syntax extension for JavaScript used within React to describe the structure of user interfaces. It allows developers to write HTML-like code directly within their JavaScript, making the creation and management of UI components more intuitive and readable.

Key aspects of React JSX:

  • HTML-like Syntax: JSX closely resembles HTML, using tags and attributes to define elements. This familiar syntax simplifies the process of building UI components for those accustomed to web development.
  • JavaScript Integration: While appearing like HTML, JSX is fundamentally JavaScript. You can embed JavaScript expressions, variables, and functions directly within JSX using curly braces {}.
  • React Component Structure: In React, components typically return JSX, defining the UI they render. This provides a clear and concise way to define a component's visual output.

Why use JSX instead of plain JavaScript?

Without JSX, creating UI in React requires multiple calls to React.createElement(), which makes the code longer and harder to read. JSX makes code more readable, closer to HTML, and easier to maintain.

Basic Rules of JSX

  • JSX must return a single parent element (use <div> or <></>).
  • Use className instead of class.
  • All tags must be closed (e.g., <br />).
  • JavaScript expressions must be wrapped in curly braces {}.

Example: Embedding Expressions

const user = 'Shivam';
const element = <h1>Hello, {user}!</h1>;

Example: Conditional Rendering

const isLoggedIn = true;
const element = (
  <div>
    {isLoggedIn ?
      <h2>Welcome Back!</h2> :
      <h2>Please Login</h2>
    }
  </div>
);

How to implement JSX in React

JSX can be implemented in a React project to create dynamic and interactive UI components. Here are the steps:

  • Create React App
  • Write JSX in App.jsx

Example:

import React from 'react';
const App = () => {
  const msg = 'John';
  return (<h2>Hello {msg}</h2>);
};
export default App;

Output:

React Rendering Elements

Rendering elements is the most basic concept in React. Elements are the smallest building blocks of React applications. They describe what you want to see on the screen.

What is a React Element?

A React element is a plain object describing a UI component. Unlike DOM elements, React elements are immutable and lightweight. They can represent DOM nodes or custom components.

Rendering an Element into the DOM

To render a React element, you use the ReactDOM.createRoot() method (in React 18+) and call root.render() with the element.

import React from 'react';
import ReactDOM from 'react-dom/client';

const element = <h1>Hello, world</h1>;
const root = ReactDOM.createRoot(document.getElementById('root'));

root.render(element);

Updating the Rendered Element

React elements are immutable. Once created, you cannot change their children or attributes. Instead, you create a new element and pass it to root.render(). React efficiently updates only what’s necessary in the DOM.

function tick() {
  const element = (
    <div>
      <h1>Hello, world!</h1>
      <h2>It is {new Date().toLocaleTimeString()}.</h2>
    </div>
  );
  root.render(element);
}

setInterval(tick, 1000);

Output Example:

React Only Updates What’s Necessary

React compares the new element with the previous one using its virtual DOM. It updates only the parts of the DOM that have changed, making rendering fast and efficient.

  • Efficient updates through the Virtual DOM.
  • Minimal re-renders for better performance.
  • Declarative approach makes UI predictable.

Best Practices for Efficient Rendering

  • Use Functional Components : They are lightweight and optimized for modern React.
  • Leverage Hooks: useState and useEffect simplify state and side effect management.
  • Prevent Unnecessary Renders: Use React.memo to avoid re-rendering unchanged components.
  • Key Prop: Assign unique key attributes to lists for optimized updates.
  • Stateful Components: Use stateful functional components for dynamic updates instead of manual render calls.

Working with Lists in React: A Quick Guide

React makes it easy to display collections of data using lists. Whether it’s rendering a list of users, products, or messages, React provides a clean and efficient way to work with arrays of data. To render a list in React, we will use the JavaScript array map() function. We will iterate the array using map() and return the required element in the form of JSX to render the repetitive elements. Here's a simple example that shows how to render a list of items:

  1. Using map() to Render Lists:

    The most common way to render lists in React is using the JavaScript map() function. Each element in the array is transformed into a React element.

    import React from 'react';

const users = ['Alice', 'Bob', 'Charlie'];

const UserList = () => {
  return (
    <ul>
      {users.map((user, index) => (
        <li key={index}>{user}</li>
      ))}
    </ul>
  );
};

export default UserList;

    Output:

  2. Rendering Lists of Objects:

    Often, your data will be in the form of objects rather than simple strings.

    const products = [
  { id: 1, name: 'Laptop', price: '$1200' },
  { id: 2, name: 'Smartphone', price: '$800' },
  { id: 3, name: 'Tablet', price: '$600' }
];

const ProductList = () => {
  return (
    <div>
      {products.map(product => (
        <div key={product.id}>
          <h3>{product.name}</h3>
          <p>{product.price}</p>
        </div>
      ))}
    </div>
  );
};

    Output

  3. Conditional Rendering in Lists:

    You can also conditionally render elements within a list using ternary operators.

    const messages = [
  { id: 1, text: 'Hello!', read: true },
  { id: 2, text: 'How are you?', read: false }
];

const MessageList = () => {
  return (
    <ul>
      {messages.map(message => (
        <li key={message.id}>
          {message.text} {message.read ? '(Read)' : '(Unread)'}
        </li>
      ))}
    </ul>
  );
};

    Output

List with a Click Event

A 'List with a Click Event' in React typically refers to displaying a list of items (such as an array) on the screen, where each item is associated with an event handler (such as onClick) that executes a function when the item is clicked.

const App = () => {
  const COMPANY = ['Welcome', 'To', 'LearnCode'];
  const handleClick = (COMPANY) => {
    alert(`You clicked on ${COMPANY}`);
  };

  return (
    <ul>
      {COMPANY.map((COMPANY, index) => (
        <button key={index} onClick={() => handleClick(COMPANY)}>
          {COMPANY}
        </button>
      ))}
    </ul>
  );
};
export default App;

Importance of Keys in React Lists

In React, each item in a list should have a unique key prop. Keys help React identify which items have changed, are added, or removed. This improves performance and avoids unnecessary re-renders.

const users = ['Alice', 'Bob', 'Charlie'];

const UserList = () => {
  return (
    <ul>
      {users.map(user => (
        <li key={user}>{user}</li>
      ))}
    </ul>
  );
};

Working with Forms in React: A Quick Guide

React applications utilize forms to gather user input, similar to standard HTML forms. However, React introduces a distinct approach to managing form data, primarily through "controlled components."

1. Controlled Components

A controlled component is a form element whose value is tied to the component’s state.

import React, { useState } from "react";

const SimpleForm = () => {
  const [name, setName] = useState("");

  const handleChange = (event) => setName(event.target.value);

  const handleSubmit = (event) => {
    event.preventDefault();
    alert(`Hello, ${name}!`);
  };

  return (
    <form onSubmit={handleSubmit}>
      <label>
        Name:
        <input type="text" value={name} onChange={handleChange} />
      </label>
      <button type="submit">Submit</button>
    </form>
  );
};

export default SimpleForm;

Output

2. Multiple Inputs

Use a single state object to manage multiple inputs:

const MultiInputForm = () => {
  const [formData, setFormData] = useState({ email: "", password: "" });

  const handleChange = (event) =>
    setFormData({ ...formData, [event.target.name]: event.target.value });

  const handleSubmit = (event) => {
    event.preventDefault();
    console.log(formData);
  };

  return (
    <form onSubmit={handleSubmit}>
      <input type="email" name="email" value={formData.email} onChange={handleChange} placeholder="Email" />
      <input type="password" name="password" value={formData.password} onChange={handleChange} placeholder="Password" />
      <button type="submit">Login</button>
    </form>
  );
};

Output

3. Uncontrolled Components

Sometimes, you don’t need to manage every input via state. You can use refs:

import React, { useRef } from "react";

const UncontrolledForm = () => {
  const nameRef = useRef();

  const handleSubmit = (event) => {
    event.preventDefault();
    alert(`Hello, ${nameRef.current.value}!`);
  };

  return (
    <form onSubmit={handleSubmit}>
      <input type="text" ref={nameRef} placeholder="Enter name" />
      <button type="submit">Submit</button>
    </form>
  );
};

export default UncontrolledForm;

Output

4. Controlled vs Uncontrolled Components

FeatureControlled ComponentUncontrolled Component
Value ManagementState (via useState)Ref (via useRef)
ValidationEasy and flexibleLess control
Updates on InputImmediate (onChange updates state)Only accessed on submit
ComplexitySlightly more verboseSimple for small forms

5. Best Practices

  • Always prevent default form submission using event.preventDefault().
  • Controlled components are recommended for complex forms.
  • Consider libraries like Formik or React Hook Form for large applications.
  • Validate inputs and provide user feedback.

ReactJS Keys

A key serves as a unique identifier in React, helping to track which items in a list have changed, been updated, or removed. Keys are particularly useful when dynamically creating components or when users modify the list.

1. Using Keys in a List

const items = ['Apple', 'Banana', 'Cherry'];

const ItemList = () => (
  <ul>
    {items.map((item, index) => (
      <li key={index}>{item}</li>
    ))}
  </ul>
);

Output

2. Without Keys (Warning)

If you render a list without a key prop, React will show a warning in the console: "Each child in a list should have a unique 'key' prop." This can lead to inefficient re-rendering and unexpected behavior.

const ItemList = () => (
  <ul>
    {items.map((item) => (
      <li>{item}</li> // Warning: Missing key prop
    ))}
  </ul>
);

Output

3. Props vs Keys

FeaturePropsKeys
PurposePass data from parent to child componentsIdentify elements in a list for React's reconciliation
Accessible in componentYes, via propsNo, React uses keys internally; not accessible via props
Required?Only when passing dataRecommended when rendering lists
